exampleAnswers.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing a Constant on One Side

question.explanation:
First, we use the power rule to simplify the right-hand side. This gives

\begin{align*} \log {(x - 2)} &= \dfrac{1}{4}\log(256) \\[3pt] \log {(x - 2)} &= \log \left(256^{1/4}\right) \\[3pt] \log {(x - 2)} &= \log (4). \end{align*}

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

\begin{align*} \log {(x - 2)} &= \log (4) \\[3pt] x - 2 &= 4 \\[3pt] x &= 6. \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=6$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log {(x - 2)} &=\log {(6-2)} \\[5pt] &=\log {(4)} \\[5pt] &=\log {(256^{1/4})} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac 14\log {(256)}.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=6$ is a valid solution.

example.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing a Constant on One Side

question.explanation:
First, we use the power rule to simplify the right-hand side. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_2 {(2x -5)} &= \dfrac{1}{3}\log_2 (27) \\ \log_2 {(2x -5)} &= \log_2 (27^{1/3}) \\[3pt] \log_2 {(2x -5)} &= \log_2 (3). \end{align*}

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_2 {(2x -5)} &= \log_2 (3) \\[3pt] 2x - 5 &= 3 \\[3pt] 2x &= 8 \\[3pt] x &= 4. \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=4$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_2 {(2x -5)} &=\log_2 {(2(4) -5)} \\[5pt] &=\log_2 {(3)} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\log_2 (27).\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=4$ is a valid solution.

example.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing a Constant on One Side

question.text: If $ \log_5 {(4 - x)} =2\log_5 2,$ then what is the value of $x?$
question.explanation:
First, we use the power rule to simplify the right-hand side. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_5 {(4 - x)} &= 2\log_5 2 \\[3pt] \log_5 {(4 - x)} &= \log_5 2^2 \\[3pt] \log_5 {(4 - x)} &= \log_5 4. \end{align*}

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_5 {(4 - x)} &= \log_5 4 \\[3pt] 4 - x &= 4 \\[3pt] x &= 0. \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=0$ back into the original equation, we get

\begin{align*} \log_5 {(4 - x)} &= \log_5 {(4 - 0)} \\[5pt] &= \log_5 {(4)} \\[5pt] &= \log_5 {(2^{2})} \\[5pt] &= 2\log_5 {2}.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=0$ is a valid solution.

question.text: Given that $\log(3x-5)=\log (7-x),$ what is the value of $x?$
question.explanation:
Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

\begin{align*} \log(3x-5)&=\log (7-x) \\[3pt] 3x-5&=7-x \\[3pt] 4x&=12 \\[3pt] x&=3. \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=3$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log(3(3)-5)&\stackrel{?}{=}\log (7-3)\\[5pt] \log(4)&=\log (4)\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=3$ is a valid solution.

example.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing Linear Arguments on Both Sides

question.explanation:
Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

\begin{align*} \log (4x)&=\log (5x+9)\\[3pt] 4x &= 5x+9 \\[3pt] x &= -9. \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=-9$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log (4x)&\stackrel{?}{=}\log (5x+9)\\[5pt] \log (4(-9))&\stackrel{?}{=}\log (5(-9)+9)\\[5pt] \log (-36)&\stackrel{?}{=}\log (-36)\\[5pt] \end{align*} However, $\log (-36)$ is not a real number.

Therefore, we conclude that the equation has no real solutions.

exampleAnswers.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing Nonlinear Arguments

question.explanation:
Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_2(x^2+7)&=\log_2(2x^2+8) \\[3pt] x^2+7&=2x^2+8 \\[3pt] x^2&=-1. \end{align*}

The equation $x^2=-1$ has no real solutions. Therefore, our original logarithmic equation has no solutions either.

example.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing Nonlinear Arguments

question.explanation:
Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_{6}{(x^2 + 20)} &= \log_{6}{(-10x - 5)} \\[3pt] x^2 + 20 &= -10x - 5 \\[3pt] x^2 + 10x + 25 &= 0 \\[3pt] (x+ 5)^2 & = 0 \\[3pt] x & = -5 . \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=-5$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_{6}{(x^2 + 20)} &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_{6}{(-10x - 5)}\\[5pt] \log_{6}{((-5)^2 + 20)} &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_{6}{(-10(-5) - 5)}\\[5pt] \log_{6}{(45)}&=\log_{6}{(45)}.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=-5$ is a valid solution.
